title: How We Build, Test, Sign, and Publish GlusterFS Packages
summary: A look inside the Eliware release process: source tracking, package validation, clean-container tests, signed repositories, provenance, and immutable runtime images.
author: Eliware
content:
# How We Build, Test, Sign, and Publish GlusterFS Packages

A package appearing in a repository is not proof that it is ready to run a storage cluster. Compilation can succeed while installation, service startup, peer formation, volume creation, or client access still fails.

The Eliware GlusterFS Repository exists to make the path from upstream source to usable package and runtime image more repeatable and more inspectable. We publish EL10-compatible RPMs, supported Debian-family repositories, runtime images, and the metadata needed to understand what went into a published generation.

The process is deliberately staged:

```text
source revision
      ↓
package build
      ↓
package smoke test
      ↓
clean-environment validation
      ↓
signing and repository publication
      ↓
provenance and immutable image reference
```

Each stage answers a different question. Passing one stage does not make the others redundant.

## Upstream first

Eliware does not replace the upstream GlusterFS project. GlusterFS is an open-source distributed filesystem maintained through the Gluster community and its source repositories. The Eliware layer packages, validates, and distributes selected GlusterFS builds for environments where obtaining a current, compatible artifact is otherwise inconvenient.

The current package set includes GlusterFS 11.2 runtime components for the project’s EL10-oriented image and repository work. Upstream version, distribution target, build inputs, and Eliware package metadata are recorded separately so an operator can distinguish the software version from the distribution process that produced the artifact.

For upstream source, releases, and project documentation, use the official [GlusterFS GitHub repository](https://github.com/gluster/glusterfs), [release history](https://github.com/gluster/glusterfs/releases), and [Gluster documentation](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/).

## Stable and rolling lanes

The repository supports two useful release approaches:

- stable artifacts follow released GlusterFS versions and are intended for predictable installations;
- rolling artifacts follow upstream development and are intended for evaluation and testing.

A rolling build is not a promise that every upstream change is production-ready. It is a way to make upcoming work available to people who need to test it before the next stable release. Rolling artifacts should be clearly labeled and should not be mixed into a stable installation accidentally.

Both lanes use the same general discipline: record the source revision, build the target packages, run validation, preserve the result, and publish only after the relevant gates pass. The difference is the source and release policy, not whether rolling work gets tested.

## The Conductor coordinates the release

The local release coordinator, called the Conductor, checks the inputs required for a build before scheduling expensive work. That includes source revisions, supported base images, repository storage, signing configuration, and external service availability.

If a required input cannot be verified, the coordinator stops before scheduling work that cannot be completed reliably. This is a small but important behavior: an unavailable signing key, missing base image, or unreachable publication destination should not look like a successful build with a problem discovered only at the end.

The Conductor also keeps release metadata in one place and uses checkpoints for the expensive stages. Package work, validation, image work, provenance, and publication can be resumed where appropriate instead of rebuilding every successful stage after an interruption.

## Package smoke testing

The first validation stage runs close to the package build. The freshly generated packages are installed into the builder environment and exercised through a basic GlusterFS lifecycle.

The point is not to reproduce every possible customer workload. It is to catch immediate failures such as:

- packages that cannot be installed together;
- missing runtime dependencies;
- services that do not start;
- commands that are absent or unusable; and
- a basic volume lifecycle that cannot complete.

A package that cannot pass its local smoke test does not proceed as if it were a valid release candidate.

## Clean-environment validation

A builder environment contains caches, source trees, tools, and state that can hide packaging mistakes. The second stage installs the candidate into a clean distribution container and tests it as a new user would encounter it.

That test exercises the essential storage lifecycle:

1. install the candidate packages;
2. start the required GlusterFS services;
3. form the test peer relationship;
4. create and start a test volume;
5. mount or access the volume;
6. write and read test data; and
7. remove the test resources.

This stage is intentionally separate from compilation. A package that worked in the builder but fails in a clean environment has not passed the release gate.

## Runtime-image validation

Packages and container images have different failure surfaces. An image can contain the expected RPMs and still fail because of its entrypoint, filesystem layout, permissions, environment handling, network behavior, or service supervision.

The final image receives its own lifecycle test. The test checks that the image contains the expected runtime components and can complete the core GlusterFS storage flow. The image is not treated as validated merely because its package inputs were validated earlier.

This separation also makes rebuilds more efficient. If a package candidate already passed its package gates and only the image needs to be regenerated, successful package checkpoints can be reused. Conversely, a new package candidate must pass its own gates even if an older image was healthy.

## Provenance is part of the artifact

A version number alone does not answer the questions operators have during an incident or audit. The release process records relationships among:

- the upstream source revision;
- operating-system and base-image inputs;
- generated package candidates;
- validation outcomes;
- repository metadata;
- signing results;
- image references; and
- immutable image digests.

This makes it possible to ask practical questions:

- Which source revision produced this package?
- Which distribution input was used?
- Did the package pass a clean-environment lifecycle test?
- Which image digest corresponds to this release?
- Which validation stage passed before publication?

The goal is not to create paperwork for its own sake. It is to make the published artifact easier to inspect, reproduce, and discuss.

## Signing and publication

After the relevant gates pass, the pipeline signs repository metadata and packages according to the configured release process. Published repositories contain the indexes, checksums, provenance records, and release reports associated with the generation.

The repository HTTP service serves the resulting publication tree. It is intentionally read-only and stateless: repository content lives in shared publication storage rather than being baked into the service image. Multiple HTTP replicas can therefore serve the same generation without rebuilding the presentation layer for every package update.

This separation also makes the security boundary clearer. The public service distributes artifacts and metadata. It is not the release coordinator, signing authority, or administrative control plane.

## Immutable image references

Tags are useful for humans, but a deployment that needs reproducibility should record an immutable image digest. The Eliware image workflow preserves the digest alongside the release metadata so an operator can identify the exact image content used by a deployment.

That does not mean every image is suitable for every workload. It means that when you test or deploy a selected image, you can refer to the exact content rather than relying only on a mutable label.

The same principle applies to the base image used to build the application image. The project’s local build expects a published immutable base-image digest rather than silently falling back to an untracked local substitute.

## Why GlusterFS builds GlusterFS

There is a satisfying loop in the project: GlusterFS-backed storage supports the build workspaces, validation workflow, publication storage, and repository website that distribute GlusterFS.

The pieces have different responsibilities:

```text
GlusterFS source
      ↓
package builders
      ↓
Gluster-backed build workspaces
      ↓
validation, signing, provenance
      ↓
Gluster-backed publication storage
      ↓
glusterfs.eliware.org
```

The builders use persistent storage for workspace continuity, logs, and compiler caches, while expensive compilation can use local scratch space. The storage layer provides persistence; the builders provide compute; the Conductor provides coordination; and the repository service provides distribution.

That circularity is useful only because the boundaries are explicit. We are not claiming that a storage system validates itself by existing. We are using the same project in a real workflow and testing the specific paths that workflow depends on.

## What this process does not guarantee

A successful release gate does not guarantee:

- that every workload will perform well;
- that a replica volume is a backup;
- that a Kubernetes deployment is correctly networked;
- that a local failure test covers every production failure;
- that a rolling build is production-ready; or
- that operators can skip capacity planning, monitoring, or recovery tests.

Validation narrows uncertainty. It does not remove the need for an operator to understand the deployment and workload.

The project is experimental, and deployment artifacts remain environment-specific. We would rather state that plainly than turn a package test into a claim about every possible production topology.

## How to evaluate a published artifact

When choosing an artifact, check:

1. whether it belongs to the stable or rolling lane;
2. which distribution and architecture it targets;
3. which GlusterFS source version it contains;
4. whether the repository metadata and packages are signed;
5. which validation results accompany the generation;
6. which immutable image digest applies, if using a container; and
7. whether the artifact matches the network, filesystem, and security requirements of your environment.

Install a candidate in a disposable test environment first. Create a small volume, test client access, stop a node, observe healing, and verify the logs and readiness behavior before placing important data on it.

## A practical promise

The Eliware repository is built around a modest promise: make GlusterFS artifacts easier to obtain, easier to inspect, and easier to evaluate on current infrastructure.

That means publishing more than a tarball or a package filename. It means tracking the source, testing the lifecycle, signing the result, preserving provenance, and making the exact image content identifiable.

For an installation walkthrough, start with [GlusterFS on EL10: Install It and Create Your First Replica-3 Volume](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/). To understand the operational layer built around the artifacts, read [Managing GlusterFS Without Losing the CLI](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/). For upstream project information, visit the [Gluster community](https://www.gluster.org/community/).
